## Page 1: ATimeofWarIntro

### Full · `atimeofwarintro.mp3` · 451 words

> My father was a genius! I state this now, not with the naïveté of my initial discovery of his journal, but as a time-tested statement of truth. It is why I pen these words today for posterity and to affirm with deep conviction what some may erroneously refer to as mad science.
>
> When I first arrived at my father's manor, I carried the same skepticism any normal individual would. Weary as I was from the excursion across the Hungarian plains, the cold, gray walls of the villa with its oppressive iron gates chilled me to my marrow. When the disfigured caretaker — the only person privileged with the knowledge — revealed to me a false door and spiraling staircase that descended to a secret laboratory, the grim discovery did nothing to soothe my nerves. In fact, the sight of jars filled with preserved flesh and the astringent stench of chemicals aggravated my frail state, leaving me to take my suppers in the bedroom for several weeks.
>
> But, it was this same dark discovery that eventually roused me from my illness. For as I pored over the journal bequeathed to me and surveyed page after page of formulaic experimentation, my apprehensions melted. I felt trepidacious, yet unreservedly enthusiastic at the ethical implications of this great task!
>
> Yet even after the disquiet within my soul was relieved, the nearby village rattled my window panes with cacophonous revelry. At first, I kept my visits to the borough brief and infrequent. It seemed that whenever I turned my head I would lock eyes with a cautious observer, and I felt the entire town's steel gaze like daggers tickling the back of my skull. I could only speculate that my siblings endured the same sordid treatment.
>
> It was my spouse, using my extended rest to become better acquainted with the village, who explained how spirited political discourse was the source of this commotion. Then I could discern the rally cry of their evening demonstrations as they spoke of disobedience, the end of monarchy, and civil war.
>
> I began to realize the potential boon that war could provide for my research. If the people shared a mere fraction of the passion that now stoked the fires of my heart, how easily they would embrace my scientific assistance! While my father's ambitions were strong, his solitary existence had doomed his ideas to obscurity.
>
> I would not repeat this error. I would brave the jeers of the populace to guide them in the art of warfare. My efforts would determine the course of this conflict. And when the time comes, it will be my science that will emerge from the flames of war as the true victor!

> My father was a genius! I say this now, not with the innocence I had when I first found his journal, but as a truth that has passed the test of time. That is why I write these words today, for the future, and to say with deep belief that this is not what some people wrongly call mad science.
>
> When I first arrived at my father's big house, I did not believe in any of it, like any normal person. I was tired from the trip across the Hungarian plains, and the cold, gray walls of the house with its heavy iron gates made me cold to the bone. The caretaker, whose face was badly damaged, was the only person who knew the secret. He showed me a hidden door and a spiral staircase that went down to a secret laboratory. This dark discovery did not calm my nerves at all. In fact, the jars full of preserved flesh and the sharp smell of chemicals made my weak health worse, and I ate my dinners in my bedroom for several weeks.
>
> But it was this same dark discovery that finally woke me from my illness. As I read the journal he had left me, page after page of formulas and experiments, my worries melted away. I was nervous, but I also felt great excitement about what this important work meant for right and wrong!
>
> But even after my soul was calm again, the village nearby shook my windows with its loud celebrations. At first, my visits to the town were short and not very often. It seemed that every time I turned my head, my eyes met the eyes of someone watching me carefully, and I felt the hard looks of the whole town like knives touching the back of my head. I could only guess that my brothers and sisters were treated in the same unpleasant way.
>
> My spouse used my long rest to get to know the village better, and explained to me that lively political discussions were the reason for all this noise. Then I could understand the cries of their evening protests, when they spoke of disobedience, the end of the king's rule, and civil war.
>
> I started to understand how useful a war could be for my research. If the people had even a small part of the passion that now burned in my heart, how easily they would accept my scientific help! My father had great ambitions, but because he lived alone, nobody ever knew about his ideas.
>
> I would not make this mistake again. I would be brave and accept the people laughing at me, to teach them the art of war. My work would decide how this conflict goes. And when the time comes, it will be my science that comes out of the flames of war as the real winner!

## Page 2: IntroMartial-Monarchists

### Full · `intromartial-monarchists.mp3` · 331 words

> If one can call the prospect of perpetual conflict stabilizing, my life settled into a somewhat steady routine. During the day, the sound of distant gunfire rumbled through the halls of my estate as silver plumes of smoke billowed beyond the mountainous horizon, casting tendril-like shadows across the land — a constant reminder of civil war. At night, the rare spectacle of an explosion brightening the sky surprised me with how viscerally I reacted.
>
> Soldiers in their bright regalia keep watch over the town from a newly erected outpost, waving the brilliant orange flag of royalty. The Monarchy had claimed victory from afar after stationing their ranks across the region, but as scuffles remained constant, this declaration was all pomp without substance. The Monarchy drafted citizens into their ranks and levied penalties against those who showed disloyalty.
>
> The inference that one of my standing should owe a debt of servitude to those who already tax my earnings into oblivion was enough to make me spill my tea. And to what end, I wondered? Could peace be mustered in a populace kept so distant from the individuals who ruled it? It was called the industrial revolution for a reason, was it not?
>
> But, I must admit, the safety that the Monarchy afforded appealed to my pocketbook. Appeasing the Monarchy would ensure money and influence, but it also appeared — for better or ill — that royalty was distant enough to take little interest in our experimentations unless they provided direct benefit to themselves, whereas the Separatists were interested in knowledge and were desperate to explore all scientific options available to them to turn the tide. However, their frail sensibilities would not so easily accept my experimentations.
>
> Ah, to be left to one's own devices or to be famously scrutinized, reviled, and revered in equal measure! The decision weighed upon me so heavily it gave me mild indigestion during my evening banquets. What direction should I choose to advance my most important scientific work?

### Easy · `intromartial-monarchists-easy.mp3` · 355 words

> If you can call the idea of a war that never ends stable, then my life became quite regular. During the day, the sound of guns far away moved through the halls of my house, while silver clouds of smoke rose behind the mountains and threw long, thin shadows across the land, always reminding us of the civil war. At night, I was surprised by how strongly I reacted to the rare sight of an explosion that lit up the sky.
>
> Soldiers in their bright uniforms watch over the town from a new outpost, waving the bright orange flag of the royal family. The Monarchy had said they won, from far away, after placing soldiers all across the region. But the small fights did not stop, so this statement was all show and nothing real. The Monarchy made citizens join the army and punished those who were not loyal.
>
> The idea that someone of my position should owe service to the people who already take almost all of my money in taxes made me spill my tea. And for what, I asked myself? Could there be peace among people who are kept so far from the people who rule them? There was a reason it was called the industrial revolution, wasn't there?
>
> But I must admit, the safety that the Monarchy gave was good for my money. Keeping the Monarchy happy would bring money and influence, and it also seemed, for better or worse, that the royal family was far enough away to not be very interested in our experiments, unless they helped the royals directly. The Separatists, on the other hand, were interested in knowledge and desperately wanted to try every scientific option they had to change the course of the war. But their sensitive feelings would not easily accept my experiments.
>
> Ah, to be left alone, or to be famous and watched, hated, and admired all at the same time! The decision was so heavy for me that it gave me a little stomach pain during my evening dinners. Which direction should I choose to move my most important scientific work forward?

## Page 3: IntroMartial-Separatists

### Full · `intromartial-separatists.mp3` · 299 words

> The length and difficulty of my journey was exacerbated by the ongoing conflict. Compounding this harried inconvenience, my spouse and I suffered the indignity of a lengthy interrogation by soldiers of the Separatist forces, who had imposed an unofficial martial government.
>
> Peasants-turned-soldiers in their motley uniforms keep watch over the town from a newly erected outpost waving a sanguine flag. They spoke of freedom as they dug fresh graves in the cemetery; the wrought iron gates perpetually wreathed in lilies. I observed the daily horse-drawn carts, dragging the wounded towards ill-equipped infirmaries; my crimson reflection in the muddy ruts of unpaved highways.
>
> It was both in spite of and because of this brashness that I found myself drawn to the scrappy Separatist upstarts and their eagerness to fight for the capricious whims of the great unwashed. The Separatists were desperate for the advantages that my family's experimentations provided, and while hesitant over our methods, were willing to further our knowledge in return. Unfortunately, this relationship made them more entitled to levy accusations towards us.
>
> However, the influence of the throne was still absolute. If one could ingratiate themselves with the distracted Monarchy, their influence and money was on offer. The peasantry would be too discontent to focus on our more "ambitious" works. Unfortunately, unless experimentation directly benefited them, the Monarchy had no use for it.
>
> Ah, to be left to one's own devices or to be famously scrutinized, reviled, and revered in equal measure! The decision weighed upon me so heavily that I could scarcely enjoy my afternoon pastries. Neither could the muffled wailing coming from the cellar laboratory nor the distant clattering of gunfire at night calm my weary mind. What direction should I choose to advance my most important scientific work?

## Page 4: MonarchReignIntro

### Full · `monarchreignintro.mp3` · 252 words

> Influence is gained in two ways: through money (that alluring and insidious scratch) and through bloodshed. Though my years on this foul Earth are few, in this abbreviated time I have learned this one valuable truth.
>
> The voracious objections of the townsfolk had become so commonplace that to see them reduced to sneering murmurs was a marked improvement that made my excursions to the village supremely more tolerable. The Separatist movement had dissipated with time, which put an end to this exasperating (yet lucrative) warring business and the peasantry returned to their normal state of impotent discontent.
>
> By this time, our family's influence had bent the ear of the throne. With keen use of investment capital, we were afforded an advisory position that could be employed to sway official opinion and deal with regional matters. This presented a delicate balance: As long as our work went unnoticed, we could avoid all consequences and remain influential. Once noticed, however, we could never return to the same peace once afforded. Heavy is the head that wears the crown, as the bard says.
>
> I was excited at the proposition, and instructed my servants to be at their finest for potential visitors; because while I grew lethargic at the thought of entertaining clerical matters of the crown, I fully recognized the power that one could wield with proper control of the state. And whether I had to bury them in gold or watch the rivers run red with blood, I would be afforded that power!

## Page 5: WarningIntro

### Full · `warningintro.mp3` · 414 words

> While the discovery of my family's experiments and journals would cement my scientific ambitions for years to come, I had never actually met them. I was too young to remember the disappearance of my brilliant progenitor. To lose a parent and then another to the subsequent dementia that followed was more folly than one child should ever have to bear. I was shielded from this reality, rushed away to Vienna, where I was consumed by my studies until my twenty-first year. It was only at my partner's insistence that I decided to settle my inheritance.
>
> I remember being stunned as I arrived by train on a mid-summer's evening. I do not know what I expected from the anecdotes my nanny had relayed to me, but it  was not the bustling cityscape that greeted me. As the sun dipped into the forest, the glimmer of modern steel light fixtures amplified the urban luminescence. My delighted spouse and I enjoyed a quiet ride in our steamer car which offered us a chance to observe the idyllic community and decidedly pleasant folk enjoying the convenience of electricity and steam turbine technology.
>
> The estate appeared untouched by years of vacancy; recently pruned brambles and ivy adorned the iron gate and the expansive grounds were immaculate. A caretaker of great age and a small housekeeping staff greeted us. Although updating the grounds to the more modern standard of the nearby town would prove a daunting task, the servants’ warm reception allayed our remaining anxieties. Upon discovery of my family's laboratory, what had been planned as a mere visit received an indefinite extension.
>
> However, when I spoke of my family's history of experimentation, I was rarely met with indifference but more often firm words of encouragement. It appeared that this region, so rife with abnormal progress, viewed my theories as rudimentary but delightfully avant-garde. Even when I expounded upon dark rituals and the grotesque, they encouraged further exploration and referred me to the newly constructed University.
>
> This caused me severe consternation. Was this not what I wanted — a clear path towards scientific enlightenment and support of my family's landmark ideas? Why did their lack of friction vex me so? Did they view my illustrious work as trivial?
>
> It was this grim realization that strengthened my will. If these craven modernists wanted more, then so be it! I would push the limits of science further than ever before and damn the consequences!

### Easy · `warningintro-easy.mp3` · 434 words

> Finding my family's experiments and journals would decide my scientific plans for many years, but I had never really met them. I was too young to remember when my brilliant ancestor disappeared. Losing one parent, and then the other to the madness that followed, was more than one child should ever have to carry. They protected me from this truth and sent me quickly to Vienna, where I was busy with my studies until I was twenty-one. Only because my partner insisted did I decide to take care of my inheritance.
>
> I remember how surprised I was when I arrived by train on an evening in the middle of summer. I do not know what I expected from the stories my nanny had told me, but it was not the busy city that welcomed me. As the sun went down behind the forest, the shine of modern steel lamps made the city lights even brighter. My happy spouse and I enjoyed a quiet ride in our steam car, which gave us a chance to see the perfect community and the very friendly people, who enjoyed the comfort of electricity and steam machines.
>
> The house looked as if all the years without anyone living in it had not touched it. The plants on the iron gate had just been cut, and the large gardens were perfect. A very old caretaker and a few house servants welcomed us. It would be a big job to make the house as modern as the town nearby, but the servants' warm welcome took away our last worries. When we found my family's laboratory, what had been planned as a short visit became a stay without an end.
>
> But when I talked about my family's history of experiments, people were rarely uninterested. More often they encouraged me strongly. It seemed that in this region, which was so full of unusual progress, people thought my theories were simple but wonderfully new and daring. Even when I talked about dark rituals and horrible things, they told me to explore further and sent me to the new University.
>
> This troubled me very much. Was this not what I wanted, a clear path towards scientific understanding and support for my family's important ideas? Why did it annoy me so much that nobody was against me? Did they think my great work was unimportant?
>
> It was this dark understanding that made my will stronger. If these cowardly modern people wanted more, then they would get it! I would push the limits of science further than ever before, whatever the consequences!

> I arrived just in time for the festivities. The normally dour gothic architecture was festooned with brightly colored ribbons, balloons, and pots overflowing with borscht. The conquering soldiers paraded down the cobblestone streets in formation and uniform, ticker tape celebrating the Separatists’ victory. Such a remarkable contrast between the slipshod militias of my youth and the democratic revolutionaries cheering the Hungarian name in time with each stomp of a soldier's boot.
>
> However, it was not this boring pageantry that ignited an infernal passion within me, it was the passion of the people. Emboldened by their conquest of a royal power and enlivened with pride in their country, this righteous fervor became a frenzy.
